resources.name: Location, biophysical and agronomic parameters for croplands in northern Ghana
resources.description:
Abstract

    Smallholder agriculture is the bedrock of the food production system in sub-Saharan Africa. Yields in Africa are significantly below potentially attainable yields for a number of reasons, and they are particularly vulnerable to climate change impacts. Monitoring of these highly heterogeneous landscapes is needed to respond to farmer needs, develop an appropriate policy and ensure food security, and Earth observation (EO) must be part of these efforts, but there is a lack of ground data for developing and testing EO methods in western Africa, and in this paper, we present data on (i) crop locations, (ii) biophysical parameters and (iii) crop yield, and biomass was collected in 2020 and 2021 in Ghana and is reported in this paper. 

    In 2020, crop type was surveyed in more than 1800 fields in three different agroecological zones across Ghana (the Guinea Savannah, Transition and Deciduous zones). In 2021, a smaller number of fields were surveyed in the Guinea Savannah zone, and additionally, repeated measurements of leaf area index (LAI) and leaf chlorophyll concentration were made on a set of 56 maize fields. Yield and biomass were also sampled at harvesting. LAI in the sampled fields ranged from 0.1 to 5.24 m² m⁻², whereas leaf chlorophyll concentration varied between 6.1 and 60.3 µg cm⁻². Yield varied between 190 and 4580 kg ha⁻¹, with an important within-field variability (average per-field standard deviation 381 kg ha⁻¹). 

    The data are used in this paper to (i) evaluate the Digital Earth Africa 2019 cropland masks, where 61% of sampled 2020/21 cropland is flagged as cropland by the data set, (ii) develop and test an LAI retrieval method from Earth observation Planet surface reflectance data (validation correlation coefficient R=0.49, root mean square error (RMSE) 0.44 m² m⁻²); (iii) create a maize classification data set for Ghana for 2021 (overall accuracy within the region tested: 0.84), and (iv) explore the relationship between maximum LAI and crop yield using a linear model (correlation coefficient R=0.66 and R=0.53 for in situ and Planet-derived LAI, respectively). 

    The data set, made available here within the context of the Group on Earth Observations Global Agricultural Monitoring (GEOGLAM) initiative, is an important contribution to understanding crop evolution and distribution in smallholder farming systems and will be useful for researchers developing/validating methods to monitor these systems using Earth observation data.

resources.name: Reference Dataset for Land Use Change Mapping in Ghana's Cocoa Landscape (2024–2025)
resources.description:
This dataset was produced by the Centre for Remote Sensing and Geographic Information Services (CERSGIS) as part of the project Reference Data Collection for Improving Land Use Change Mapping in Ghana. The primary objective was to develop high-quality reference data to enhance the accuracy of remote sensing-based land use and land cover (LULC) change mapping using machine learning methods in Ghana’s cocoa production landscapes.
The dataset comprises:

  • cocoa_farms: 21,031 geocoded cocoa farm polygons, including agroforestry and shadeless cocoa plots - collected using OpenForis Ground
    • homogeneous_cocoa_farm: 14,192 homogeneous cocoa polygons (shadeless) digitised from total cocoa plots
  • other_land_uses: 20,035 additional geocoded points and polygons representing informal gold mining, degraded forest, oil palm (commercial and subsistence), and rubber (commercial and subsistence) - collected with Collect Earth Online
  • gha_cocoa_hh_public: 485 anonymised cluster records derived from 4,444 individual household survey that complement the geospatial data and provide socioeconomic context - collected with KoboToolbox

This dataset provides a critical foundation for automated land cover classification and change detection models in tropical forested regions, where land use is heterogeneous and dynamic. It was developed to support researchers, policymakers, and practitioners across sub-Saharan Africa engaged in monitoring commodity-driven deforestation, landscape restoration, and sustainable land management.
This dataset was originally created with support from Lacuna Fund, the world’s first collaborative effort to provide data scientists, researchers, and social entrepreneurs in low- and middle-income contexts globally with the resources they need to produce labelled datasets that address urgent problems in their communities. Lacuna Fund is a funder collaborative that includes The Rockefeller Foundation, Google.org, Canada’s International Development Research Centre, the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) with GIZ as implementing agency, Wellcome Trust, Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, Patrick J. McGovern Foundation, and The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. See https://lacunafund.org/about/ for more information.

Please contact fmensah@ug.edu.gh with any questions or report an issue on Github here. Let us know how you plan to use the dataset. We are very interested in potential collaborations.

NOTE: The cocoa farm geospatial data does not represent property or farm boundaries and should not be used for compliance / legal purposes. This data was collected for the purposes of training remote sensing models for improved mapping of cocoa and other land covers, and not for geolocating specific farms for the purposes of compliance with any regulation. Field data collectors did not trace property boundaries in the field, and field data was checked for quality and potentially edited in GIS. Therefore, these polygons represent only portions of cocoa farms. The sizes of cocoa polygons in this dataset do not necessarily relate to the size of an entire farm for a given location

resources.name: Modelling Water Stress in a Shiraz Vineyard Using Hyperspectral Imaging and Machine Learning
resources.description: The detection of water stress in vineyards plays an integral role in the sustainability of high-quality grapes and prevention of devastating crop loses. Hyperspectral remote sensing technologies combined with machine learning provides a practical means for modelling vineyard water stress. In this study, we applied two ensemble learners, i.e., random forest (RF) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), for discriminating stressed and non-stressed Shiraz vines using terrestrial hyperspectral imaging. Additionally, we evaluated the utility of a spectral subset of wavebands, derived using RF mean decrease accuracy (MDA) and XGBoost gain. Our results show that both ensemble learners can effectively analyse the hyperspectral data. When using all wavebands (p = 176), RF produced a test accuracy of 83.3% (KHAT (kappa analysis) = 0.67), and XGBoost a test accuracy of 80.0% (KHAT = 0.6). Using the subset of wavebands (p = 18) produced slight increases in accuracy ranging from 1.7% to 5.5% for both RF and XGBoost. We further investigated the effect of smoothing the spectral data using the Savitzky-Golay filter. The results indicated that the Savitzky-Golay filter reduced model accuracies (ranging from 0.7% to 3.3%). The results demonstrate the feasibility of terrestrial hyperspectral imagery and machine learning to create a semi-automated framework for vineyard water stress modelling.

resources.name: A feature selection approach for terrestrial hyperspectral image analysis
resources.description: Feature selection techniques are often employed for reducing data dimensionality, improving computational efficiency, and most importantly for selecting a subset of the most important features for model building. The present study explored the utility of a Filter-Wrapper (FW) approach for feature selection using terrestrial hyperspectral remote sensing imagery. The efficacy of the FW approach was evaluated in conjunction with the Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) classifiers, to discriminate between water-stressed and non-stressed Shiraz vines. The proposed FW approach yielded a test accuracy of 80.0% (KHAT = 0.6) for both RF and XGBoost, outperforming the more traditional Kruskal-Wallis (KW) filter by more than 20%. The FW approach was also less computationally expensive when compared with the more commonly used Sequential Floating Forward Selection (SFFS) wrapper. Additionally, we examined the effect of hyperparameter optimisation on classification accuracy and computational expense. The results showed that RF marginally outperformed XGBoost when using all wavebands (p = 176) and optimised hyperparameter values. RF yielded a test accuracy of 83.3% (KHAT = 0.67), whereas XGBoost yielded a test accuracy of 81.7% (KHAT = 0.63). Our results further show that optimising hyperparameter values yielded an overall increase in test accuracy, ranging from 0.8% to 5.0%, for both RF and XGBoost. Overall, the results highlight the effect of feature selection and optimisation on the performance of machine learning ensembles for modelling vineyard water stress.

resources.name: A Scoping Review of Landform Classification Using Geospatial Methods
resources.description: Landform classification is crucial for a host of applications that include geomorphological, soil mapping, radiative and gravity-controlled processes. Due to the complexity and rapid developments in the field of landform delineation, this study provides a scoping review to identify trends in the field. The review is premised on the PRISMA standard and is aimed to respond to the research questions pertaining to the global distribution of landform studies, methods used, datasets, analysis units and validation techniques. The articles were screened based on relevance and subject matter of which a total of 59 articles were selected for a full review. The parameters relating to where studies were conducted, datasets, methods of analysis, units of analysis, scale and validation approaches were collated and summarized. The study found that studies were predominantly conducted in Europe, South and East Asia and North America. Not many studies were found that were conducted in South America and the African region. The review revealed that locally sourced, very high-resolution digital elevation model ( DEM) products were becoming more readily available and employed for landform classification research. Of the globally available DEM sources, the SRTM still remains the most commonly used dataset in the field. Most landform delineation studies are based on expert knowledge. While object-based analysis is gaining momentum recently, pixel-based analysis is common and is also growing. Whereas validation techniques appeared to be mainly based on expert knowledge, most studies did not report on validation techniques. These results suggest that a systematic review of landform delineation may be necessary. Other aspects that may require investigation include a comparison of different DEMs for landform delineation, exploring more object-based studies, probing the value of quantitative validation approaches and data-driven analysis methods.

resources.name: Scoping the Field: Recent Advances in Optical Remote Sensing for Precision Viticulture
resources.description: The use of passive optical remote sensing (RS) has a rich history in precision viticulture (PV), with the use of RS technologies being employed in a myriad of PV applications. The present work undertakes a scoping review to examine past and current trends in the use of RS in grapevine production. It aims to identify literature gaps and new research opportunities. The Scopus database facilitated the search for relevant articles published between 2014 and 2023 using a search string of keywords. A total of 640 articles were produced by the Scopus search. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) reporting framework, the 640 articles were reviewed based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, resulting in 388 articles being deemed eligible for further data extraction. Four research questions were defined to guide the data extraction process, and a coding scheme was implemented to address these questions. The scoping review found Italy and the United States to be leading contributors to the research field, with vineyard mapping, yield estimation, and grapevine water status being the most extensively studied RS–PV applications. However, the use of RS to map vineyard soil properties and grapevine cultivars remains underexplored, presenting promising avenues for future research.

resources.name: Mapping the spatial profile and susceptibility of illegal land occupation: A case study of the Cape Town Metropolitan area, South Africa
resources.description: Illegal land occupation has become a major challenge to sustainable development in urban areas1 . Developing countries, such as South Africa, experience a greater incidence of illegal land occupation due to rapid urbanisation, high unemployment rates, and shortages in land ownership amongst historically disadvantaged individuals (Hendricks & Pithouse 2013.; Mkhize 2014). Illegal land occupation presents various environmental hazards, impedes effective governance, and contributes to economic losses (Mutero & Makwara 2018). Analysing the spatial characteristics of illegal land occupation can drive effective policy development, deter illegal land use cases, and help determine areas susceptible to illegal land invasions. However, limited research has been done on the spatial dynamics of illegal land occupation. The absence of comprehensive spatial information pertaining to illegal land occupation is, therefore, the primary motivation for this research. This abstract presents a preliminary case study on the Cape Town Metropolitan Area and aims to map land areas' susceptibility to an illegal land invasion.

resources.name: Analysis of Ceilometer LiDAR (CL51) Sensor Atmospheric Profile Images for Urban Environmental Monitoring Over Pretoria, South Africa
resources.description: Clouds are a critical component of the atmosphere, influencing both climate and weather patterns, while their backscatter impacts human activities and lives. The CL 51 Ceilometer LiDAR is one of the advanced atmospheric sensors deployed globally to collect massive data for monitoring environmental conditions. This sensor captures data in digital format, which is subsequently converted into images. However, extracting atmospheric features, such as aerosol distribution along the sensor's path length, requires precise identification for effective analysis. In this paper, we outline the methodology for data acquisition, conversion to image format, and feature extraction of atmospheric components from the CL 51 script. We further analyse the atmospheric images derived from CL 51 seasonal data collected in Pretoria from 2014 to 2015. This analysis of CL 51 ceilometer LiDAR images will enhance our knowledge and understanding of the atmospheric aerosol profile, thereby contributing to urban environmental monitoring efforts.

resources.name: Image Quality Assessment Methods for Near-Infrared Wildfire Imagery
resources.description: Over the past two decades, there has been a surge of interest in the study of image quality assessment due to its broad applicability in many fields. Satellites and other remote sensing applications have been collecting vital data that is utilised to monitor targets or events in varying environmental conditions all over the world. Some of these collections include images of natural disasters and anthropogenic events such as wildfires, floods, and drought, among others. However, appropriate image quality assessment techniques have been lacking for image fusion and other remote sensing applications where the information is not targeting the human visual system. Currently, there are several perceptual image quality assessment methods that can be applied depending on the image sensor type. In this paper, we focus on various no-reference general and specific image quality methods that can be used to evaluate remote sensing images for fire detection. Further, we evaluate the effectiveness of the non-referential image quality techniques applied in the processing of airborne sensor images, notably those for fire detection, and correlate the effectiveness of these techniques to the accuracy of detection. In this paper Image quality assessment (IQA) methods such as entropy, BRISQUE, MUSIQ, exposure, and CPBD are analyzed along with methods for image distortion, i.e., Gaussian blur, and image enhancement such as HE, AHE, and CLAHE. Therefore, the no-reference image quality assessment investigation will contribute to the detection and correction of image quality processing issues in wildfires.

resources.name: Enhanced mapping of a smallholder crop farming landscape through image fusion and model stacking
resources.description: Globally, Smallholder farming systems (SFS) are recognized as one of the most important pillars of rural economic development and poverty alleviation because of their contribution to food security. However, support for this agricultural sector is hampered by lack of reliable information on the distributions and acreage of smallholder fields. This information is essential in not only monitoring food security and informing markets but also in guiding the determination of levels of support required from government by individual farmers. There is urgent need for robust techniques that can be used to cost-effectively and time-efficiently map smallholder crop fields especially in Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. This study attempts to do this by using an approach in which optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data are systematically combined and classified using Extreme Gradient Boosting (Xgboost). We also investigated model stacking as another technique to improve classification accuracy. We combined Xgboost with Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), and Naïve Bayes (NB). The combined use of multi-temporal Sentinel-2 bands, spectral indices, and Sentinel-1 produced better results than exclusive use of optical data (α = 0.95, p = 0.0005). Furthermore, stacking of classification algorithms based on model comparisons achieved higher accuracy than stacking the algorithms indiscriminately (α = 0.95, p = 0.0100). Through systematic fusion of SAR and optical data and hyper-parameter tuning of Xgboost, we achieved a maximum classification accuracy of 97.71%, while achieving a maximum accuracy of 96.06% through model stacking. This highlights the importance of multi-sensor data fusion and multi-classifier systems when mapping fragmented agricultural landscapes.

resources.name: Do Satellite Data Correlate with In Situ Rainfall and Smallholder Crop Yields? Implications for Crop Insurance
resources.description: Adverse weather is one of the most prevalent sources of risk in agriculture. Its impacts are aggravated by the lack of effective risk management mechanisms. That is why resource-poor farmers tend to respond to weather risks by adopting low-capital investment, low-return, and low-risk agricultural practices. This challenge needs to be addressed with innovative risk management strategies. One of the tools that is gaining traction, especially in the developing countries, is weather-index-based insurance (WII). However, WII uptake is still low because of several constraints, one of which is basis risk. This study attempts to address this problem by evaluating the suitability of TAMSAT, CHIRPS, MODIS, and Sentinel-2 data for WII. We evaluated the first three datasets against in situ rainfall measurements at different spatial and temporal scales over the maize-growing season in a smallholder farming area in South Africa. CHIRPS had higher correlations with in situ measured rainfall data than TAMSAT and MODIS NDVI. CHIRPS performed equally well at 10 km and 25 km spatial scales, and better at monthly than daily and 16-day time steps (maximum R = 0.78, mean R = 0.72). Due to the lack of reliable historical yield data, we conducted yield surveys over three consecutive seasons using an objective crop cut method. We then assessed how well rainfall and NDVI related with maize yield. There was a poor relationship between these variables and maize yield (R2 ≤ 0.14). The study concludes by pointing out that crop yield does not always have a linear relationship with weather and vegetation indices, and that water is not always the main yield-limiting factor in smallholder farming systems. To minimize basis risk, the process of designing WII must include identification of main yield-limiting factors for specific localities. Alternatively, insurers could use crop water requirement methods to design WII.

resources.name: A Proposed Satellite-Based Crop Insurance System for Smallholder Maize Farming
resources.description: Crop farming in Sub-Saharan Africa is constantly confronted by extreme weather events. Researchers have been striving to develop different tools that can be used to reduce the impacts of adverse weather on agriculture. Index-based crop insurance (IBCI) has emerged to be one of the tools that could potentially hedge farmers against weather-related risks. However, IBCI is still constrained by poor product design and basis risk. This study complements the efforts to improve IBCI design by evaluating the performances of the Tropical Applications of Meteorology using SATellite data and ground-based observations (TAMSAT) and Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data (CHIRPS) in estimating rainfall at different spatial scales over the maize-growing season in a smallholder farming area in South Africa. Results show that CHIRPS outperforms TAMSAT and produces better results at 20-day and monthly time steps. The study then uses CHIRPS and a crop water requirements (CWR) model to derive IBCI thresholds and an IBCI payout model. Results of CWR modeling show that this proposed IBCI system can cover the development, mid-season, and late-season stages of maize growth in the study area. The study then uses this information to calculate the weight, trigger, exit, and tick for each of these growth stages. Although this approach is premised on the prevailing conditions in the study area, it can be applied in other areas with different growing conditions to improve IBCI design.

resources.name: A Satellite-Based Crop Insurance That Compensates for Rainfall Deficit
resources.description: There is urgent need for innovative solutions that can be used to reduce the devastating impacts that extreme weather has on agriculture. Index-based crop insurance (IBCI) promises to be a capable tool that can be used to this end. However, the widespread adoption of IBCI is hindered by basis risk, which plagues many IBCI designs. This study uses satellite-based rainfall estimates (SRFE) and weather station-based evapotranspiration (WSE) data to design an IBCI model for maize. The SRFEs estimate rainfall with high accuracy at 20day and monthly time steps and are then combined with WSE data to design an IBCI model. The model covers the (1) development, (2) mid-season, and (3) late-season stages of maize. We then formulate IBCI thresholds including the weight, trigger, exit and tick, for each of the above-listed growth stages. This approach can be tested in other areas with different growing conditions and alternative sources of rainfall and evapotranspiration data.

resources.name: Monitoring changes in land-use and land-cover to ascertain the nature, causes and extent of degradation in the savannahs of Raymond Mhlaba Local Municipality, Eastern Cape, South Africa
resources.description: Multi-date Landsat images were used to ascertain the nature, causes and extent of degradation in the savannahs of Raymond Mhlaba Local Municipality in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa by comparing changes in land-use and land-cover in one commercial farm and two communal areas over a period of 30 years between 1984 and 2014. Results revealed a persistent increase in bush encroachment, persistent decrease in grassland in all areas, and abandonment of arable farming in communal areas. The paper concludes by providing strategies to change the adverse effects of these changes.

resources.name: Integration of geospatial-based algorithms for groundwater potential characterization in Keiskamma Catchment of South Africa
resources.description: Groundwater supports over 2.4 billion people across the globe and is critical to food security. The spatial dynamics of groundwater vary from place to place. The irregularity of groundwater resource exploitation is recognized in drought-prone areas, putting pressure on the resource. Hence, accurate groundwater potential characterization is critical for sustainable development and management of groundwater, particularly in drought-prone environments. Therefore, this study aimed at utilizing remote sensing satellite data and geospatial-based (analytical hierarchy process (AHP) and frequency ratio (FR)) algorithms to characterize groundwater potential zones (GWPZs) in the Keiskamma Catchment of South Africa. Seven (7) selected factors, including geology, soil type, slope, rainfall, drainage density, lineament density, and land use land cover, were assigned weights based on the AHP and FR algorithms. The validation results showed that the FR model performed better than the AHP, with the area under curve (AUC) accuracies of 62% and 50%, respectively. Based on the findings of this study, we infer that FR is more reliable than AHP when characterizing GWPZ. Lastly, GWPZ maps produced will be beneficial for improving efficient planning, management strategies, and decision-making.

resources.name: Dataset of Spatial Distribution of Rainfall–Runoff and Water Area of Typical Lakes and Reservoirs in the Lancang–Mekong River Basin
resources.description:
The Lancang–Mekong River runs through the Greater Mekong Subregion. The section within China is called the Lancang River, while the downstream section outside China is known as the Mekong River. It is one of the most important international rivers in the China–ASEAN region, and issues related to water resource utilization and ecological environment protection have attracted significant international attention. At present, there is still insufficient understanding of the temporal variability and long-term trends of water resources in this basin. Monitoring and analyzing changes in basin surface runoff and the water areas of major lakes and reservoirs are therefore of great significance for ecological and environmental protection in the Lancang–Mekong River Basin and the surrounding countries.
The remote sensing data used in this dataset are mainly derived from Chinese satellite observations. The sensors include the CCD sensors onboard China’s HJ-1A and HJ-1B environmental satellites (HJ-1A/CCD1, HJ-1A/CCD2, HJ-1B/CCD1, and HJ-1B/CCD2), with a spatial resolution of 30 m. Based on these data, a runoff product with a spatial resolution of 30 m was generated for the period June 2013 to May 2014. In addition, the dataset analyzes variations in water area and water storage of several typical lakes and reservoirs in the region, including Tonle Sap Lake, Nam Ngum Reservoir, Ubol Ratana Reservoir, and Sirindhorn Reservoir.
The compressed dataset size is 7.56 MB, and it is fully open for sharing..

resources.name: Dataset of 5 km Resolution Solar Total Radiation in the Belt and Road Region and Adjacent Areas （2015）
resources.description: Based on data from the Japan Meteorological Agency's geostationary satellites MTSAT-2/Himawari-8 in 2015, the European Space Agency's MSG2/MTG satellites, China's FY2E/FY2F data, MODIS atmospheric products (including water vapor products MOD05/MYD05, cloud products MOD06/MYD06, and aerosol products MOD04/MYD04), and the 16-day composite MODIS surface albedo product (MCD43C2), a lookup table algorithm based on a radiative transfer model was employed. First, a cloud mask was created, and different lookup tables were selected based on clear or cloudy conditions to generate instantaneous solar radiation, which was then accumulated into daily average solar radiation. Subsequently, monthly and annual solar radiation were calculated, resulting in a 5 km resolution dataset of total solar radiation for the Belt and Road region and its adjacent areas (2015). Compared with 12,485 sets of observed solar radiation values, the overall correlation coefficient was 0.93, the overall bias was 10.13 W/m² (5.86%), and the root mean square error was 35.83 W/m² (20.72%). The data results indicate that the total solar radiation in the Belt and Road region and its adjacent areas in 2015 ranged from 3,551 to 8,583 MJ/m², with an average of 6,400 MJ/m². Spatially, total solar radiation was higher in Africa, West Asia, South Asia, and Oceania, while it was lower in eastern and northern China, most of Europe, and Russia. The dataset consists of a single .tif file with a spatial resolution of 5 km and a data volume of 78.3 MB (compressed to 9.09 MB).

resources.name: Fire risk index
resources.description: This dataset is a fire risk index product for areas prone to wildfires globally. Specifically, it is an 8-day composite, 500-meter spatial resolution fire risk index product for five regions: southwestern China, northern Australia, southern Europe, central Africa, and the west coast of the United States from 2000 to 2018. This dataset provides reference data on fire risks for scientific research on areas prone to wildfires globally and for fire prevention departments. During the period from 2000 to 2018, the area of forest burned areas globally ranged from 60 million hectares to 97 million hectares, with significant interannual fluctuations. The relatively concentrated distribution areas mainly include central and southern Africa, northern Australia, and the central and northern parts of South America. Among them, the area of forest burned areas in Africa accounts for more than 60% of the global total. Fires have a significant impact on forest net primary productivity. In the year of the fire, the forest net primary productivity shows a significant decline and generally gradually recovers within the next three to four years. Among the five regions prone to forest fires globally, there is no obvious trend change in the forest fire risks in northern Australia and southern Europe. Although the forest fire risks in southwestern China, central Africa, and the west coast of the United States remain at a relatively high level, they show a weak downward trend.

resources.description: For the global Leaf Area Index (LAI) dataset spanning 2010 to 2020, suitable single-scattering albedo values and relative uncertainty levels were designated for different vegetation types to enhance the global applicability of the 3D radiative transfer model. Subsequently, a lookup table was constructed based on the improved 3D stochastic radiative transfer model to retrieve LAI values. Finally, a meteorological data-driven neural network method was adopted to fill the missing LAI data caused by the degradation of remote sensing observation data quality due to multiple factors (including weather conditions, atmospheric conditions and sensor malfunctions), thereby generating a long-term and continuously observed LAI product.

resources.name: Global Urban Land Composite and Expansion in 2000-2020
resources.description: Since the beginning of the 21st century, cities around the world have developed rapidly. According to a UN report, 4.22 billion people lived in cities in 2018, accounting for 55% of the global population. It is projected that the global urbanization rate will reach 68% by 2050. Urban expansion and land cover changes are important aspects for measuring the quality of urban living environment, ecosystem services and even human well-being. High-precision remote sensing monitoring of urban subsurface on a global scale can provide scientific understanding and decision-making basis for achieving the United Nations' 2030 Sustainable Development Goal of "building inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable cities and communities". Satellite remote sensing technology was adopted to monitor the global urban expansion and land cover changes over the past two decades. Supplemented by socio-economic statistics and other data, the spatio-temporal patterns and differentiation laws of the expansion of 9 megacities and 1,468 typical cities around the world were analyzed. The distribution characteristics and changing trends of urban land cover in different regions were revealed, and the urban areas of different countries with different land resource endowments and income levels were evaluated The configuration differences of municipal green Spaces offer suggestions for the sustainable development of global cities in the future. In terms of time scale, it has been expanded to the second decade of the 21st century. In terms of monitoring content, information on urban land cover (referring to coverage types such as urban impervious water surfaces, green Spaces and water areas) has been added, forming a remote sensing mapping product for global urban expansion and land cover changes in the past two decades. Monitoring results show that the global urban land area has increased from 239,000 square kilometers in 2000 to 519,800 square kilometers in 2020, an expansion of 280,800 square kilometers. The impervious surface area of global cities has grown rapidly, increasing from 153,000 square kilometers in 2000 to 311,900 square kilometers in 2020. The area of global urban green space has significantly increased, from 65,400 square kilometers in 2000 to 171,600 square kilometers in 2020, and its proportion of urban land area has risen from 27.36% to 33.01%. The compiled data mainly come from Landsat, HJ, ZY, GF, DMSP/OLS, NPP/VIIRS, socio-economic statistics and urban planning materials, etc. By applying big data, machine learning and human interaction interpretation methods, three series of global urban expansion and land cover data for the years 2000, 2010 and 2020 were generated According to the product.

resources.name: Belt and Road 1km Resolution Light-Temperature-Water Stress Factor Anomaly Dataset (2015)
resources.description: The spatial distribution differences of light, temperature, and water stress factors in the "Belt and Road" land areas are significant. North of 20°N and south of 25°S, the influence of light and temperature stress factors increases with increasing latitude. The influence of water stress factor is greatest around 22°N and 22°S, gradually decreasing towards the north and south with latitude change. In the cold temperate and frigid zones north of 40°N in Eurasia, the climate is cold, and vegetation growth is primarily constrained by temperature and light. In high-altitude regions such as the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, Pamir Plateau, Hindu Kush Mountains, Taurus Mountains, Tianshan Mountains, Kunlun Mountains, etc., vegetation growth is primarily constrained by temperature. In western Europe and southern East Asia, the climate is mild and humid, and vegetation growth is primarily constrained by light. In tropical, subtropical, and temperate desert regions between 40°N and 40°S, including the Arabian Peninsula and Iranian Plateau in West Asia, the Indian Peninsula in South Asia, the Turan Lowland in Central Asia, the Junggar Basin, Turpan Basin, and Tengger Desert in East Asia, and the Western Desert region of Australia, the climate is dry, and vegetation growth is primarily constrained by water. In tropical rainforest regions near the equator, such as the Congo River Basin in Central Africa, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, New Guinea in Southeast Asia, and Madagascar Island in Southern Africa, rainfall and heat coincide, precipitation is abundant, light, temperature, and water conditions are sufficient, and vegetation growth is not constrained by light, temperature, or water factors.

resources.name: 2014 African Land Cover Mapping
resources.description: Africa is one of the fastest-growing continents in the world, where timely understanding of ecological and environmental changes is essential to support global change research. The 2014 African Land Cover Map is developed based on multi-source satellite remote sensing data, establishing the most up-to-date African land cover database and conducting monitoring of changes in key land cover types and regions. Building on the analysis of land cover area statistics for African countries in 2014, 13 countries are selected for comparative land cover assessment based on criteria including land area, Gross Domestic Product (GDP), population, and foreign economic and trade relations. To investigate significant land cover changes and their environmental impacts in Africa, four typical regions are chosen to analyze land cover dynamics between 2000 and 2014. These include cropland changes in the lower Nile River basin, forest changes in the eastern Congo Basin, urban expansion around Lake Victoria, and grassland changes in the Sahel region. The compressed data volume of this dataset is 3.58 GB, and it is made available through fully open access sharing.

resources.name: The Vegetation Coverage Datasets Covering Ten Interconnection Projects of the Belt and Road Initiative
resources.description: Against the backdrop of the Belt and Road Initiative, the impact of major interconnection infrastructure projects invested in or constructed by China overseas on the local environment has attracted widespread attention from the international community. This paper selects 10 major interconnection projects and uses remote sensing technology and Landsat-8 remote sensing images to produce a dataset of vegetation coverage within the 10km buffer zone along each project. This dataset is based on Landsat-8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) optical images. First, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is calculated on the Google Earth Engine cloud platform, and then the maximum NDVI of the study area in 2017 is synthesized. Using this data as the base, the vegetation coverage dataset is calculated by the pixel dichotomy model method. The value of vegetation coverage ranges from 0 to 1. 0 indicates no vegetation coverage, and a higher value indicates a better degree of vegetation coverage.

resources.name: Global Large Terrestrial Surface Water Areas Spatially Distributed Update Dataset (2018-2019)
resources.description: Land surface waters often exist in liquid forms such as rivers, lakes, reservoirs and transitional waters, and are an important part of the global water cycle, participating in the natural cycle of matter and energy. The spatial distribution of land surface water reflects to some extent the storage and utilization of land surface water resources, and its fluctuations or changes reflect the impact of climate fluctuations and changes, surface processes and human activities on the water cycle, material migration and ecosystem changes. The temporal and spatial distribution characteristics of land surface waters and their dynamic changes profoundly affect global ecology, economy and human well-being. In the context of global warming, a series of significant changes have occurred in the spatiotemporal characteristics of global land surface waters, which not only affect the service functions of aquatic ecosystems, but also pose a significant threat to ecological security. Therefore, time series monitoring of global land surface water area, revealing interannual and seasonal variations of land surface water in different regions of the world, is an important foundational task for promoting research on the global water cycle, strengthening water resources management, responding to global environmental changes, and implementing global ecological environment health diagnosis. Based on the 8-day synthetic reflectance product of the Medium resolution imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Terra and Aqua with a spatial resolution of 500 meters from 2018 to 2019, the dynamic water mapping update of key global lakes was obtained using the rule-based automatic process of water mapping. The "Update of Large land surface water area spatial distribution data" was evaluated using the method of generating true value maps from high-resolution remote sensing data. The dataset was divided into Sinusoidal Tile Grid, 46 times a year, and was stored in *.tif format, including annual water coverage.

resources.name: Boundaries and Remote Sensing Classification Dataset for Major International Wetlands (2001, 2013)
resources.description: Wetlands are among the most biodiverse and productive ecosystems globally. Based on the Ramsar Wetland Convention website, protected area information, and other supplementary materials, this dataset delineates the boundaries of 100 large (area greater than 200,000 hectares) internationally important wetlands worldwide by referencing high-resolution remote sensing imagery such as Google Earth and Tianditu. Using the 250-meter spatial resolution, 16-day composite MOD13Q1 products from the Terra/Aqua satellites' MODIS sensor for the years 2001 and 2013 as the primary data source, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) was filtered and reconstructed into time series. The Support Vector Machine (SVM) method was applied for classification and mapping, resulting in a remote sensing classification dataset for the 100 internationally important wetlands in 2001 and 2013. Compared with high-resolution remote sensing imagery and literature data, this wetland remote sensing classification dataset effectively reveals the spatiotemporal changes in wetlands within internationally important sites under the dual influences of climate fluctuations and human activities. It demonstrates greater advantages over wetland monitoring based on single-period remote sensing data. The dataset can serve as a reference for wetland conservation, management, and global environmental change research. The compressed dataset size is 102 MB, and it is fully open-access for sharing.

resources.name: Dataset of the effects of typical major droughts on terrestrial vegetation
resources.description: Drought is a persistent, anomalous precipitation deficit—a state of surface water imbalance where water supply fails to meet normal demand. Different relationships between supply and demand lead to different types of drought (meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, and socio-economic). A drought disaster occurs when this drought hazard interacts with vulnerable entities (such as agriculture, pastoral systems, urban areas, and ecosystems) within a specific disaster-prone environment (comprising both natural and human-influenced settings), resulting in harm to those exposed elements. Based on the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), the Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT), GLASS Leaf Area Index (LAI) product, and Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (FAPAR) product, this study employed anomaly analysis and spatial statistical methods to investigate the impacts of the 2001 drought in the North China Plain and surrounding areas, the 2007 drought in the southeastern United States, and the 2009–2010 drought in southwestern China on different terrestrial vegetation types.

resources.description: The Global Land Surface Satellite (GLASS) data products are independently developed by the research team led by Professor Liang Shunlin from Beijing Normal University. GLASS products are long-term and high-precision global land surface remote sensing products retrieved based on multi-source remote sensing data and in-situ measurements. These products provide a reliable basis for the study of global environmental change and can be widely used in the dynamic monitoring of atmosphere, vegetation cover, water bodies and other aspects at global, continental and regional scales. Combined with climate change characteristic parameters such as air temperature and precipitation, they can provide sound scientific, technical and data support for the study of global ecological environment evolution, ecological environment monitoring, resource development and socio-economic sustainable development. This dataset is stored in HDF and XML formats, in which the data entities are stored in HDF files, and the metadata information of the products is stored in both HDF and XML files. resources.description: Similar to the spatial distribution of sea surface temperature, the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in the marine areas along the "Belt and Road" generally decreases with increasing latitude. However, affected by factors such as cloud cover, PAR exhibits spatial differences in sea areas at the same latitude but different longitudes. For example, the PAR in the eastern marine areas of China is significantly lower than that in the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean at the same latitude. PAR in these 12 marine areas shows significant seasonal variations: the maximum PAR in mid-to-high latitude marine areas occurs in June or July, and the minimum in December or January; tropical marine areas usually have two peak values of PAR, appearing in March–April and September–October respectively. In terms of the amplitude of seasonal variation, the largest variation is located in European marine areas, while the variation in tropical marine areas is relatively small.

resources.name: Dataset of Global Land Degrading and Improving Assessment at 500 m (2000-2018)
resources.description:
（1）From 2000 to 2018, the two processes of global land degradation and restoration occurred simultaneously in different regions with almost equal total areas, and land degradation in arid and semi-arid areas showed a significant restoration trend. This indicates that remarkable achievements have been made in global desertification prevention and control since the implementation of the UNCCD.
Since 2000, the total area of land with aggravated and expanded degradation worldwide has reached 16.0959 million km², accounting for 11.95% of the global land area; the total area of restored and improved land is 16.4762 million km², accounting for 12.23% of the global land area, with the restored area slightly larger than the degraded one. Areas with aggravated and expanded land degradation are concentrated in the tropics and southern regions of Africa and South America, while restored and improved land is mostly distributed in Asia, North America and other regions.
As a sensitive area to land degradation, the area of land with aggravated degradation in global arid and semi-arid regions has reached 2.7850 million km² since 2000. In the same period, 4.3406 million km² of land in these regions has been restored and improved, with the restored area being about 56% higher than the degraded one—far exceeding the global average level of land degradation and restoration. This reflects the remarkable achievements in global desertification prevention and control since the implementation of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD). Monitoring and analysis results show that Asia has the largest area of restored and improved land in arid and semi-arid regions, accounting for more than 50% of the total restored area, with China and India contributing the most to such restoration.
（2）Since the beginning of this century, large-scale forest degradation in important global tropical rainforest areas has posed new challenges to the achievement of the SDG targets for land degradation neutrality, which must arouse widespread attention from the international community and relevant countries.
Since 2000, large-scale forest degradation has occurred in global tropical rainforest regions with optimal hydrothermal conditions such as the Amazon Plain and the Congo Basin. This is closely related to consecutive droughts caused by global warming and El Niño under the background of global change, as well as extensive deforestation, reclamation and frequent fire disturbances. The large-scale, high-intensity degradation in these non-traditional land degradation areas has posed new challenges to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets for land degradation neutrality, which must arouse widespread attention from the international community and relevant countries.
（3）In major traditional global land degradation areas, the trend of land degradation has been significantly reversed in regions such as China and the South Asian subcontinent. This indicates that effective policy guidance and proactive scientific governance actions can effectively reverse the trend of land degradation, and Asia's experience provides a valuable reference for global land degradation prevention and control.
Since 2000, in major traditional global land degradation areas, the trend of aggravated and expanded land degradation has been evident in the Sahel, the Ethiopian Plateau, the East African Plateau, the Brazilian Plateau, and the northern regions of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. This is mainly caused by irrational large-scale reclamation and abandonment driven by population pressure and economic interests, as well as backward agricultural infrastructure and production management models, with climate change not being the main cause of land degradation.
In the same period, among traditional global land degradation areas, the trend of land degradation has been reversed in China, the South Asian subcontinent and other regions, with significant improvement and restoration of land quality over a large area. China and India together contribute 26.78% to the global land restoration and improvement. Specifically, China has greatly improved the vegetation coverage capacity of degraded land through effective ecological engineering governance, realizing the restoration and improvement of degraded land, and contributing 19.13% to the global land restoration and improvement.

resources.description: Leaf Area Index (LAI) is defined as the total one-sided green leaf area per unit ground surface area. resources.name: Global 500m 4-day Fractional Vegetation Cover Dataset (2010-2020)
resources.description: Fractional Vegetation Cover (FVC) is defined as the ratio of the vertical projection area of vegetation canopy or leaf surface on the ground to the total area of the vegetation region. It is an important parameter for characterizing the degree of surface vegetation coverage and also one of the key indicators for reflecting changes in the ecological environment. A quantitative remote sensing inversion algorithm for FVC based on the gap probability theory is adopted to produce long time-series and high-precision FVC products. Taking the multi-day composite Leaf Area Index (LAI) and Clumping Index (CI) products as inputs, the algorithm generates the Global 500m 4-day Fractional Vegetation Cover Dataset (2010-2020) based on the gap probability theory, which has good global applicability. Compared with the ImagineS ground measured data, the algorithm accuracy of the FVC product reaches RMSE=0.13 and BIAS=-0.05, showing better consistency with the ground measured FVC data. In comparison with the GEOV1 FVC neural network algorithm and the MuSyQ FVC pixel dichotomy model estimation method, the introduction of the CI parameter to consider the vegetation structure and spatial distribution characteristics can effectively suppress the overestimation of FVC in dense vegetation areas. The dataset adopts the Sinusoidal Tile Grid for tiling, with each scene covering a latitude and longitude range of 10°×10°, and is stored in *.tif format.

resources.description: Based on the global 1km grid land cover change data set from 2015 to 2020, and the quantitative remote sensing thematic products of global 500 m/4 d ecosystem elements from 2010 to 2020. The data set includes global photosynthetically active radiation products from 2015 to 2020. Photosynthetically active radiation is the spectral component of solar radiation that is effective for plant photosynthesis. Its wavelength range is 400~700nm, and it basically coincides with visible light.

resources.description: The surface melt of the Greenland Ice Sheet is a sensitive indicator of global climate change and a major contributor to ice sheet mass loss. resources.description: This data product presents the crop water productivity of four major food crops (corn, wheat, rice, and soybean) through a geospatial grid system. Covering the years 2000-2022 with a spatial resolution of 5 km, it integrates crop yield and area data from the 5 km global food production dataset, along with 1km resolution monthly evapotranspiration remote sensing data. This quantified data on water use efficiency for major food crops provides critical insights into regional variations and underlying drivers of water utilization patterns in global food-producing regions.

resources.name: Typical Case Dataset of Major Global Flood Disasters (2018)
resources.description:
This report comprehensively considers factors such as flood extent, affected population, and disaster losses, and selects three typical events: Hurricane Florence Flood in the United States (September 2018), Niger River Flood in Nigeria (August 2018), and Shouguang Flood in Shandong Province, China (August 2018) (Figure 4-1). It analyzes the background, triggering factors, and affected situations of flood disasters, evaluates the differences in disaster response mechanisms and measures across regions, and discusses the contributions and implications of disaster prevention and mitigation measures in regions at different development levels for achieving the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (SDGs).
(1) Compared with the period 1989–2018, the frequency and losses of global flood disasters in 2018 were slightly lower. In 2018, global flood disasters were concentrated in southern Asia, eastern North America, and central Africa, occurring mainly from July to September.
(2) Structural flood prevention and mitigation measures, such as the construction of dams, reservoirs, and drainage channels, have obvious disaster reduction benefits. Regions with well-developed disaster prevention facilities, such as eastern North America and eastern Asia, are less affected by floods than the global average. In contrast, central Africa and other regions with insufficient disaster prevention facilities suffer higher impacts.
(3) Through joint collaboration of the international community, continuous strengthening of dual support in funding and technology to improve the system of flood prevention, mitigation, and relief will help achieve the goal of “building resilient infrastructure” in the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (SDGs).

resources.name: Dataset of Tropical Cyclone Idai and Subsequent Floods in Southern Africa (2019)
resources.description: Within the impact range of Tropical Cyclone Idai, the main land use/cover types in parts of three southern African countries include cropland, grassland, forestland, and urban construction land. Tropical Cyclone Idai formed over the southwestern Indian Ocean at 04:00 on March 4, 2019, then made landfall in southeastern Africa and re-entered the ocean at 04:00 on March 9. At 00:00 on March 15, the cyclone center was located approximately 25 km northwest of the city center of Beira in central Mozambique. It swept across eastern Zimbabwe from March 15 to 16, and gradually weakened and dissipated after March 16. Making landfall near Beira, central Mozambique on March 14, Tropical Cyclone Idai affected a total of 9 cities in three countries: Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Malawi. Affected by the cyclone, the daily maximum rainfall in these three countries remained around 100 mm from March 7 to 22, with the maximum rainfall exceeding 300 mm on March 15 and 16. The maximum cumulative rainfall over 16 days reached 650 mm, mainly occurring in Mozambique, with the distribution area consistent with the cyclone's landfall area, causing secondary floods in these regions. Tropical Cyclone Idai and its secondary floods caused severe disasters, particularly in Mozambique, where Beira, Buzi, and Dondo were the most severely affected.

resources.description: The monitoring area of The Belt and Road spans a vast geographic range. The 2014 distribution of forest above-ground biomass shows that the Southeast Asian region, located at low latitudes with year-round torrid temperatures, abundant perennial sunlight and precipitation, boasts rich forest resources and exuberant forest growth, dominated by tropical rainforests and tropical monsoon forests. resources.name: The Drought Degree and Its Impacts on Vegetation Dataset in North China (2011)
resources.description: Most areas in the North China Plain and its surrounding regions in China belong to the temperate semi - arid and semi - humid monsoon climate zone, with cold and dry winters and hot and rainy summers. The main vegetation types in this region include cultivated land, typical grasslands, closed shrublands, and sparse shrublands. Climate change and human activities have important impacts on the vegetation growth in this region. Most of the cultivated land in this region is irrigated. During the entire drought event, the proportions of the area where the LAI and FAPAR of the cultivated land in this region decreased compared with the multi - year average level were approximately 70% and 60% respectively. In the same period, the proportions of the area where the LAI and FAPAR of the typical grasslands decreased compared with the multi - year average level were both about 90%. This indicates that irrigation mitigates the impact of drought on the cultivated land in this region, enabling the crops on the cultivated land to have a higher ability to resist drought than the typical grasslands.

resources.name: Grid Dataset of Global Land Degradation Trend at 500 m (2000-2018)
resources.description:
Since 2000, in the traditional land degradation areas around the world, regions such as the Sahel in Africa, the Ethiopian Plateau and the East African Plateau, the Brazilian Plateau, and the northern parts of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea have shown a significant trend of degradation expansion and aggravation. This is mainly caused by unreasonable large-scale reclamation and abandonment of farmland driven by population pressure and economic interests, as well as backward agricultural infrastructure and agricultural production management models. Climate change is not the main cause of land degradation.
During the same period, in traditional land degradation areas around the world, the trend of land degradation reversed in regions such as China and the South Asian subcontinent, with significant improvement and recovery of land quality on a large scale. Among them, China has largely improved the vegetation coverage capacity of degraded land through effective ecological engineering governance (such as returning farmland to forest/grassland, closing mountains for natural regeneration, and afforestation), achieving improvement and restoration of degraded land; India has effectively curbed land degradation mainly through the implementation of the "Green Revolution", the improvement of agricultural irrigation systems and the promotion of advanced agricultural cultivation and management techniques. The achievements of China and India in the governance of large-scale land degradation provide experience and examples for the global governance of land degradation.
Unlike previous monitoring results, this report shows extensive forest degradation in tropical rainforest regions with the best water and heat conditions in the world since 2000, such as the Amazon Plain and the Congo Basin. This is mainly due to factors such as global warming, years of drought caused by El Nino, extensive deforestation, reclamation and frequent fire disturbances in the context of global change. The large-scale, high-intensity degradation in these non-traditional land degradation areas has an impact on SDG land
The achievement of degradation prevention targets poses new challenges that must be given high attention by the international community and relevant countries.

resources.name: Terra MODIS-based product of greenness dynamics of Arctic terrestrial vegetation from 2002-2021
resources.description: Arctic terrestrial vegetation exhibits a significant response to rapidly changing climate. Based on vegetation index data from the Terra MODIS satellite sensor, this product provides the annual maximum NDVI data for the Arctic terrestrial growing season from 2002 to 2021, which can be used to analyze and monitor the distribution and dynamics of Arctic vegetation. The annual maximum NDVI dataset is generated using Terra MODIS NDVI data; after preprocessing including subsetting, cloud removal, and water masking, images from the growing season (June, July, and August) of each year are used to produce annual maximum value composites. The product is validated using spatially and temporally consistent Landsat data, with an overall accuracy of 82.87% and a Kappa coefficient of 0.74 respectively. Against the background of significant changes in Arctic terrestrial vegetation, this data product can effectively monitor and assess the distribution and variation of Arctic terrestrial vegetation, and provide scientific data support for the sustainable development of the Arctic region.

resources.name: The Belt and Road 1km 5-day Normalized Difference Vegetation Index Dataset (2016-2019)
resources.description: The 1km resolution NDVI dataset in The Belt and Road region is a 5-day resolution dataset produced with reference to the standard MODIS-NDVI compositing algorithm on the basis of 5 types of 1km resolution satellite remote sensing data (Terra/MODIS, Aqua/MODIS, NOAA18/AVHRR, FY3A/VIRR, FY3B/VIRR). The compositing algorithm of this dataset consists of two steps: First, within the 5-day compositing period, the multi-source data are divided into three quality grades with residual thresholds of 10%, 20% and more than 20% by using the kernel coefficient robust fitting method based on NDVI weight, among which the third-grade data with residual threshold more than 20% have the worst quality and are not involved in compositing. Then, according to the number of valid observations of each quality grade within the 5-day compositing period, the main algorithm or backup algorithm is adopted respectively for NDVI compositing, and the NDVI time series with a temporal resolution of 5 days and a spatial resolution of 1km in The Belt and Road region from 2016 to 2019 are obtained. In the Heihe River Basin of China, high-resolution ASTER images are used to compare and analyze the dataset with the standard MODIS NDVI products. The results show that the determination coefficient R² of NDVI generated based on the multi-source dataset is significantly higher than that of the standard MODIS-NDVI generated based on the single-source dataset. The dataset adopts the Sinusoidal Tile Grid for tiling, with each scene covering a latitudinal and longitudinal range of 10°×10°, and is stored in *.tif format.

resources.name: Global 500m land surface satellite (GLASS) vegetation net primary production (NPP) dataset，2000-2018
resources.description:
Based on the 2018 global 30m resolution forest cover product, the Global 500m land surface satellite (GLASS) vegetation net primary production (NPP) dataset, 2000-2018 and other relevant products, this chapter studies the spatial distribution characteristics of the current status of forest cover and productivity at the global, climatic zone and intercontinental scales, and analyzes the correlation between the current global forest cover status and global economic and population development, as well as forest management systems and objectives.
The global forest area in 2018 was 3.815 billion hectares, accounting for 25.60% of the global land area; the NPP of forest ecosystems reached 35.283 billion tons of carbon per year, accounting for approximately 55.44% of the global vegetation NPP. The global distribution of forests across different climatic zones is unbalanced. Among them, tropical regions have the widest distribution and the largest forest area, amounting to 1.847 billion hectares, accounting for 48.40% of the global total forest area; similarly, tropical regions also have the highest total forest NPP, at 24.05 PgC yr⁻¹ (1 PgC = 1 billion tons of carbon), accounting for 68.17% of the global total forest NPP.
From an intercontinental perspective, there are significant differences in the current status of forest cover. Asia has the largest forest cover area, accounting for 30.91% of the global total forest cover area; followed by South America and North America, whose forest cover areas account for 22.29% and 20.11% of the global total forest cover area respectively. In terms of forest coverage rate, South America has the highest rate, reaching 47.66%; followed by Europe and North America, with forest coverage rates of 36.06% and 31.05% respectively. The total forest NPP of each continent in descending order is South America, Asia, Africa, North America, Europe and Oceania. The highest total forest NPP is 11.78 PgC yr⁻¹, accounting for 33.39% of the global total forest NPP; while the lowest is only 1.53 PgC yr⁻¹, accounting for 4.33% of the global total forest NPP.

resources.description: This data product presents the global cropland evapotranspiration (ET) product. It covers the years from 2000 to 2022 with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer. This dataset reveals the refined spatial distribution pattern and interannual variation characteristics of global cropland ET, providing important data support for understanding the differences in water requirements for global agricultural production and the driving mechanisms of changes. The dataset can be widely applied in the fields of global water resource assessment and agricultural water resources, offering a scientific basis for achieving the United Nations' goals of sustainable development of water resources and the water environment.

resources.name: Evapotranspiration Dataset in the Belt and Road and Surround Region (2015)
resources.description: Evapotranspiration is an important process of water movement in the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum, including evaporation and transpiration. Evaporation is the process by which water changes from a liquid or solid state to a gas state, and transpiration is the process by which water dissipates from the stems and leaves of plants into the atmosphere. The evapotranspiration products from 2010 to 2015 were produced based on remote sensing products and ECMWF atmospheric reanalysis data from the European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts. The spatial range of the evapotranspiration products covered the entire globe, with a spatial resolution of 1km and a temporal resolution of 1 day. The accuracy of the evapotranspiration products was evaluated using latent heat flux observation data from vorce-related stations. The accuracy of the products at most of the sites was above 80%.

resources.description: Forest fires are one of the most severe natural disasters, spreading rapidly and often causing enormous losses and damage. They pose a significant threat to national economic development, global ecological balance, and the safety of personal lives and property. Based on GLASS product data such as Leaf Area Index (LAI) and Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (FAPAR), combined with MODIS land cover data, MODIS MCD45 burned area products, and the global Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT) data, this study analyzes the impact of forest fires on terrestrial vegetation changes and the differences in their recovery processes. The analysis focuses on the 1987 forest fire in the Greater Khingan Range forest area of Heilongjiang Province, China, the 1988 forest fire in Yellowstone National Park, USA, and the 2009 forest fire in Victoria, southeastern Australia, using methods such as anomaly analysis and time series analysis.

resources.name: Forest Biomass Remote Sensing Retrieval Data Product for the Greater Mekong Subregion
resources.description:
The Greater Mekong Subregion is rich in forest resources. However, affected by factors such as logging, wildfires, pests and diseases, the region’s forest area has been declining overall, with natural forests decreasing at an accelerated pace in particular. On the other hand, planted forests in the region are expanding rapidly, especially industrial timber forests such as rubber and eucalyptus plantations. A large number of young and middle-aged forests have weak carbon sequestration capacity.
Forest biomass is not only the basis for estimating forest carbon storage and assessing the contribution of forests to the carbon cycle, but also an important parameter for evaluating forest ecological functions. Therefore, the analysis of forest biomass and carbon sequestration capacity using 30-meter resolution data from the Operational Land Imager (OLI) on Landsat 8 can provide a reference for improving forest quality and formulating sustainable forestry development plans.
The compressed size of this dataset is 1.89 GB, and it is fully open access.

resources.name: Belt and Road Port Cities and Their Surrounding Areas Land Cover Classification Dataset
resources.description:
In port cities across East Asia and Southeast Asia, the predominant land cover types in surrounding areas are forests and cropland, followed by impervious surfaces. Specifically, forests account for a high proportion around Busan and Kuantan, reaching over 70% (70.78% and 93.16%, respectively). In contrast, cropland dominates around Shanghai and Bangkok, with proportions of 49.38% and 79.79%, respectively. Among impervious surfaces, Singapore, Shanghai, and Bangkok exhibit higher proportions at 36.82%, 29.89%, and 15.62%, respectively.  

From an ecological perspective, the surrounding areas of East Asian cities like Shanghai are primarily characterized by cropland, while Busan is dominated by forests. In Southeast Asian port cities, forests are the dominant land cover, followed by cropland. In South Asian port cities, cropland is the main land cover type, with forests as the secondary type. West Asian port cities are predominantly surrounded by bare land. In Europe, Lisbon is mainly surrounded by cropland, whereas Saint Petersburg is dominated by forests. In the European part of the Africa-Mediterranean region, port cities are primarily surrounded by cropland, followed by forests and grasslands. In Oceania, Sydney is mainly surrounded by forests, while Darwin is dominated by grasslands, with forests as the secondary type.

resources.name: 30m resolution Global forest cover and forest change map
resources.description:
Based on the global 30 m resolution forest cover change products (2000 and 2018), the global 500 m resolution forest net primary productivity (NPP) products and other datasets, this chapter studies the spatiotemporal variation and distribution characteristics of forest cover and productivity from 2000 to 2018 from the global, climatic zone and intercontinental perspectives, and analyzes the correlation between global forest cover change and global economic development, population growth, forest management systems and management objectives since the 21st century.
Since the start of the 21st century, the global forest cover area has been generally stable with a slight decline, with a net reduction of 17 million hectares, accounting for 0.44% of the total global forest area. The increase and decrease in forest area have shown obvious regional differences. Overall, the forest cover area of high-income developed countries has remained stable or increased, while that of some low-income developing countries and regions has witnessed a sharp decline. In addition, affected by extreme climates and extensive forest exploitation, the tropical zone has seen a significant reduction in forest cover area since the 21st century, with a net loss of 57 million hectares. With the large-scale implementation of ecological restoration projects in China, the country's forest area had a net increase of 45 million hectares from 2000 to 2018, reaching a total of 212 million hectares, representing a 26.90% growth in forest cover area. China has become a major contributor to maintaining the basic balance of the global forest cover area.
The total global forest NPP has shown a slow overall downward trend, with a decrease of 463 million tons of carbon (tC) and a decline rate of 1.33%, and the NPP in forest change areas (including deforestation and afforestation) has dropped by 59 million tC. Monitoring results indicate that the regions with a sharp decline in forest NPP since 2000 are mainly concentrated in the tropical rainforest areas near the equator. Corresponding to the increase in China's forest cover area, the forest NPP in China has also risen significantly, increasing by 6.95% compared with 2000, which reflects the positive effects of China's ecological protection projects, afforestation and other initiatives on the growth of forest NPP.

resources.description: Vegetation fraction in this data product is defined as the percentage of the total statistical area occupied by the vertical projection of vegetation (including leaves, stems, and branches) on the ground surface. The dataset is presented in a geospatial grid format, covering the period from 1985 to 2023 with a spatial resolution of 500 m. It was generated using the pixel dichotomy model based on the independently produced NDVI dataset. This dataset reveals the fine spatial distribution patterns and interannual variations of vegetation growth in major global deserts and their surrounding areas. It provides decision-making support for understanding the ecological environment and desertification processes, and for implementing scientific and effective desertification control and ecological restoration in these regions.

resources.name: Global 1km 5-day Normalized Difference Vegetation Index Dataset (2010-2020)
resources.description: The Global 1km 5-day Normalized Difference Vegetation Index Dataset (2010-2020) is a 5-day resolution dataset produced with reference to the standard MODIS-NDVI compositing algorithm, based on five types of 1km resolution satellite remote sensing data (Terra/MODIS, Aqua/MODIS, NOAA18/AVHRR, FY3A/VIRR, FY3B/VIRR). The compositing algorithm of this dataset consists of two steps: First, within the 5-day compositing period, the multi-source data are divided into three quality grades according to residual thresholds of 10%, 20% and above 20% by using the kernel coefficient robust fitting method based on NDVI weight, among which the grade III data with residual threshold above 20% have the poorest quality and are not involved in the compositing. Then, the main algorithm or backup algorithm is adopted for NDVI compositing according to the number of valid observations of each quality grade within the 5-day compositing period, and the NDVI time series with a temporal resolution of 5 days and a spatial resolution of 1km across the globe from 2015 to 2020 is obtained. In the Heihe River Basin of China, high-resolution ASTER images are used to compare and analyze the dataset with the standard MODIS NDVI products. The results show that the coefficient of determination R² between the NDVI generated based on the multi-source dataset and ASTER-NDVI is significantly higher than that of the standard MODIS-NDVI generated based on the single-source dataset. The dataset adopts the Sinusoidal Tile Grid for tiling, with each scene covering a latitude and longitude range of 10°×10°, and is stored in *.tif format.

resources.name: Global Gridded Crop Production Dataset at 5km Resolution from 2000 to 2022
resources.description: This dataset presents the production of four major food crops (corn, wheat, rice, and soybeans) through a geospatial grid system, covering the years 2000-2022 with a spatial resolution of 5 kilometers. Quantifying the spatial distribution and trends of grain production, and identifying key factors limiting yield growth, are fundamental requirements for implementing effective measures to enhance food production and achieve global food security. As the first high-resolution global dataset of major crop yields, it reveals the detailed spatial patterns and interannual variations in global food crop production, providing crucial data support for understanding regional disparities and change drivers in global food production. This dataset can be widely applied in global food security assessments, agricultural production monitoring, and agricultural policy formulation, offering key scientific evidence for achieving the food security goals under the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

resources.description: Mitigating climate change at both regional and global levels and reducing carbon dioxide emissions represent one of the greatest challenges facing humanity. Areas with higher emissions are predominantly located in North China and along the eastern coastal regions, while emissions in the western and other areas remain relatively low.

resources.description: Global 500m Vegetation Growth Index Dataset (2010-2020) is a thematic dataset generated from global annual mean vegetation coverage (FVC) and annual cumulative net primary productivity (NPP) data. To address the limitations of FVC and NPP in accurately reflecting vegetation growth characteristics—particularly their focus on productivity or coverage capacity—the 2010-2020 Global 500m Annual Vegetation Growth Index product was developed. This comprehensive thematic product integrates the strengths of FVC (vegetation structure parameter) and NPP (vegetation functional parameter). The dataset employs sinusoidal projection, with each product covering a 360° x 150° latitude-longitude range, and is stored in.tif format.

resources.name: 30m Annual Maximum Vegetation Coverage Dataset for the Greater Mekong Subregion
resources.description:
The Greater Mekong Subregion features diverse climate types and complex geographical characteristics, with high vegetation coverage and abundant forest resources, resulting in a varied ecological environment. However, with urban expansion and changes in land use types, vegetation coverage has declined.
Based on 30-meter resolution CCD data from China’s HJ-1A and HJ-1B satellites (HJ-1A/CCD1, HJ-1A/CCD2, HJ-1B/CCD2), the vegetation coverage product was derived to monitor the spatial distribution and seasonal differences of vegetation coverage in the Greater Mekong Subregion from June 2013 to May 2014. This dataset is of great significance for addressing typical ecological and environmental issues between China and ASEAN.
The compressed size of this dataset is 2.04 GB, and it is made fully open access for sharing.
